# Comparing two populations {.hero #s07-two-populations}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="7"}
Seminar 7 · Paired vs independent
:::

The design decides the test, and the test decides the answer.

::: {.lede}
The worksheet gives you two-sample tests and paired tests as separate recipes. They are not interchangeable — run the wrong one on the same numbers and a real effect can vanish completely.
:::

## The same data, twice {.stage-slide #pair-intuition}

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-400}
<div id="pair-stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="pair-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="pair-frag-2"}

::: {.slide-footer}
The left picture is honest and useless: firms differ hugely from each other, and that between-firm spread drowns the effect. Pairing subtracts it away — every firm becomes its own control.
:::

## Watch the signal appear {.sim-slide #pair-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Seminar 7 · same numbers, two tests
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
before <- c(3,15,8,19,5,12,17,7,14,10,6,16,9,13,11)
after  <- c(1,13,5,17,4, 9,16,4,12, 7,5,13,7,10, 9)

ind <- t.test(after, before, var.equal = TRUE)
par <- t.test(after, before, paired = TRUE)

round(c(indep_t = ind$statistic,
        indep_p = ind$p.value,
        pair_t  = par$statistic,
        pair_p  = par$p.value), 4)
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
Identical numbers, identical difference in means of $-2.2$ — but the independent test cannot see it and the paired test finds it overwhelming. **The information was in which rows belong together, and the independent test throws that away.**
:::
